Evidence clusters into two opposing perspectives: (1) employment and anti-discrimination contexts where asking age is discouraged or unlawful [d4,d5,d7,d8], and (2) general etiquette and survey contexts where asking age may be acceptable depending on phrasing, relationship, or cultural norms [d1,d2,d3,d6,d9]. It is appropriate to ask someone their age only when the context, relationship, and phrasing are sensitive to their comfort and legal constraints. In job interviews in the United States, asking “How old are you?” is considered unlawful and exposes employers to age-discrimination risk under the ADEA [d4,d5]. Many etiquette sources also regard asking a woman her age as improper, especially someone barely known [d8], and general surveys caution that bluntly asking “How old are you?” can be seen as insensitive [d3]. Conversely, neutral or polite phrasing can make asking age acceptable in many everyday situations [d6], and cultural norms vary (e.g., in Russia it is acceptable except for older women) [d2]. Research on social norms among older adults shows disagreement, with many considering asking a co-worker’s age non-normative [d9], underscoring that appropriateness depends on context and perspective.
